proposed_edges.relationship: Williams’s Capitalism and Slavery tested on the compensation records: supported on slave-wealth in British society, qualified on decline, and set against a British Marxist pantheon that left James and Williams out (2009–2014)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read (History Workshop Journal 78, 2014). "C. L. R James and Eric Williams did not appear in their pantheon. James and Williams, in their struggle against racism and colonialism insisted on the linkage between metropole and colony … the intimate connections … between capitalism and slavery" (p. 23). "Williams never argued that slavery 'caused' the Industrial Revolution … as Nicholas Draper, Keith McClelland and I suggest in the co-authored book which documents the results of the first phase of our project on the Legacies of British Slave-Ownership (LBS), there is a move to a modified version of Williams’s thesis amongst economic historians" (p. 24); "Williams’s insight into the importance of slave-derived wealth to eighteenth-century society and culture has been greatly expanded" (p. 24). Qualifications: the modified thesis is attributed jointly to the LBS authors and set among economic historians (Pomeranz, Inikori); it is not a claim that slavery caused industrialization. The jointly written introduction to Legacies of British Slave-ownership (2014; read in part by the second research pass, without print pages) tests Williams directly: "Eric Williams' Capitalism and Slavery included four connected arguments that are critical for us"; "our findings are entirely supportive of Williams in the context of this second thesis" (slave-wealth in British society); on industrialisation "Our material cannot resolve these controversies"; and the work "complicates Williams by qualifying his 'decline' thesis". Katie Donington, a co-author, recalls that "The project foregrounded Williams's work" (Black Perspectives, 2020). Hall was the project's principal investigator (REF 2014 case study).

proposed_edges.relationship: Class as the key dynamic questioned: Hobsbawm and his fellow Marxist historians, aware of plantation economies, left “race, slavery and the Caribbean” outside their concern; gender and race proposed as analytics of capital formation (2014)
proposed_edges.map_label: Hall: after Hobsbawm, gender and race, 2014
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read (History Workshop Journal 78, 2014, a lecture at the conference "History after Hobsbawm"). He "was critical of the cultural turn"; "Feminist history, in his view, was at best interested in 'winning collective recognition'"; postcolonial approaches "were not on his radar beyond the work of Subaltern Studies" (p. 22). "Hobsbawm was well aware of the significance of plantation economies to the development of industrial capitalism" (p. 23), but "his concern, and that of his fellow Marxist historians, was not with race, slavery and the Caribbean" (p. 23); "While class was the key historical dynamic in his analytic work, gender and race have become key analytics for our 'interesting times'" (p. 24). Qualifications: a critique within a shared agenda, "connecting these insights with older Marxist traditions" (p. 22); she credits Industry and Empire on colonial markets (p. 23). Distinct from the critiques by Chakrabarty (edge_917) and Guha (edge_979).

proposed_edges.relationship: Metropole and colony made together: Birmingham abolitionists, Baptist missionaries and Jamaica, and the shift from paternalist hopes to racial thinking, 1830–1867 (2002)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own statement of the book's argument, read by the second research pass ("A Response to the Commentators", JBS 42:4, 2003): "The central argument of Civilising Subjects is that being a colonizer was part of the construction of Englishness in the nineteenth century" (p. 530); splitting the narrative between Jamaica and Birmingham meant "reasserting the gap between metropole and colony as fundamental to the maintenance of metropolitan power" (p. 534). A reader's explicit claim and her own description, read; the book is unread here. Woollacott (Connected Worlds, 2006, chapter 4, read in part): "The great strengths, in postcolonial terms, of Hall’s magnum opus include … her compelling insistence on the interconstitutive connections between colony and metropole; her interest in the historical construction of race and its connections to gender and class; and perhaps above all, her political engagement with the operation of imperialism and colonialism and their legacies." Hall (History Workshop Journal, 2014, p. 22): "As a protagonist of feminist and postcolonial work". The University of Chicago Press description: "the idea of empire was at the heart of mid-nineteenth-century British self-imagining"; by the 1860s "a harsher racial vocabulary". Woollacott notes its limit: no connections "between Jamaica and other colonies beyond Edward John Eyre’s career".

proposed_edges.relationship: Civilising Subjects praised for showing that “empire is always on top of what it rules”, but faulted for not drawing on Subaltern Studies for unrecorded colonised voices and for treating culture as propaganda rather than analysing how it disguised colonial violence (2003)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Said's review, "Always on Top" (LRB 25:6, 20 March 2003; complete text read via WebFetch extraction, no pagination). Praise: "Hall’s excellent book"; a "dialectical" history linking ideas, institutions and daily life; it shows that "empire is always on top of what it rules". Criticisms: sermons, polemics, letters and philosophy are treated alike as "evidence"; she does not draw on Ranajit Guha and the Subaltern Studies group (Woollacott 2006 quotes him: Hall "mystifyingly doesn’t draw" on them); her treatment of culture as propaganda follows John MacKenzie and neglects how culture, in Arnold, Carlyle and Dickens, insulated and disguised colonial violence. A mixed review whose criticisms are specific and methodological; he frames the book with Culture and Imperialism's "intertwined histories".

proposed_edges.relationship: Legacies of British Slave-ownership: slave-owners compensated at emancipation traced into British commerce, politics and culture, with gender and race as forces in capital formation (project from 2009; book and essay 2014; with Draper, McClelland and colleagues)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read (History Workshop Journal 78, 2014): "Since 2009 a team of historians at University College London, of whom I am one, have been investigating slave-owners" (p. 24); from "Nick Draper’s study of the compensation records" they "documented all the claimants to compensation at the time of emancipation – when twenty million pounds was paid to the slave-owners" (p. 26); slave-ownership is "a way of bringing slavery home and problematizing whiteness" (p. 25); the essay "argues that gender and race are both critical to capital formation … Classical Marxist accounts of the development of industrial capitalism need to be rethought" (abstract). The 2014 book, co-authored with Draper, McClelland, Donington and Lang, is read through its publisher abstract: "one powerful way in which Empire came home to Victorian Britain". Burnard (JWH, opening) calls it "this outstanding collection of essays". Collective work; all credits retained.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Black Jacobins as a model for analysing “metropole and colony in one lens” (2003)
proposed_edges.map_label: Metropole and colony in one lens, 2003
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own acknowledgement, read by the second research pass (JBS 42:4, 2003, p. 533): "Colonizers were made both in the metropole and on colonial sites. And, as C. L. R. James's The Black Jacobins (1938) taught us, much can be gained through the analysis of metropole and colony in one lens." A retrospective acknowledgement made in defending the book's method; it names a resource, not the origin of her project. Her 2014 essay also sets James and Williams against the British Marxist pantheon (History Workshop Journal 78, p. 23, read).

proposed_edges.relationship: Fanon’s claim that colonialism shaped the colonizers as much as the colonized frames the question of how empire was lived “at home” (2002–2003)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own statement, read by the second research pass (JBS 42:4, 2003, p. 530): "Yet if, as Frantz Fanon argued, colonialism shaped the colonizers as much as the colonized then how was this expressed in everyday culture? How was it lived 'at home' as well as in the empire?" One explicit sentence framing the project; the Fanon text is not specified. Not to be confused with edge_418 (fanon → identity), which concerns Stuart Hall.

proposed_edges.relationship: Slave-ownership reinscribed into modern British history: the Legacies of British Slave-ownership project and its database of about 46,000 compensation claims (2009–2014; with Draper, McClelland and colleagues)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read by the second research pass. REF 2014 case study (WebFetch excerpts): the ESRC project ran 1 June 2009 to 31 May 2012, led by "Professor Hall and her research associates, Dr Nicholas Draper and Dr Keith McClelland", and from "the records of the £20m paid in compensation to slave-owners in 1833" documented "the c.46,000 individual claims and awards". 2014 introduction (excerpts, no print pages): "our project is to reinscribe slave-ownership onto modern British history"; "The database digitises all the awards in the slave-compensation records of the 1830s". Hall (History Workshop Journal, 2014, p. 25, read): "a way of bringing slavery home". Lucky Valley (2024; publisher abstract) extends the work to Edward Long and "racial capitalism". Collective work; all credits retained. Distinct from the economic-history arrow, which records her argument about capital formation.

proposed_edges.relationship: A public Encyclopaedia of British Slave-ownership, accompanied by workshops with local and family historians and correspondence with descendants of slave-owners and the enslaved (2010–2013).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read by the second research pass. REF 2014 case study (WebFetch excerpts): workshops drew "mostly local and family historians from outside academia"; correspondents were "the great majority from descendants of slave-owners and the enslaved"; the online Encyclopaedia of British Slave-ownership launched on 28 February 2013 and had 137,998 visits from 108,022 unique visitors to 31 July 2013. The 2014 introduction names responsibilities "to the descendants of the enslaved people, to the descendants of the slave-owners and to other academic and non-academic constituencies" and says the project "has no position on reparations and restitution". An institutional impact statement and the team's own account; collective work. The atlas owner's separate Early Atlantic World project uses LBS-derived data; nothing from it is evidence here.

proposed_edges.relationship: Englishness as a formation of class, gender and race: imperial men, masculinities and “raced” white subjects (2002–2003)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own retrospective statement, read by the second research pass (JBS 42:4, 2003): her task was "to analyze the 'racing,' to use Toni Morrison's term, of white subjects, the ways in which Englishness needs to be understood not only as a formation of class and of gender, but also of race and ethnicity" (p. 531); the book "is about men, masculinities, and the making of 'raced' subjects" (p. 536); she concedes to Holt and Levine that "There is undoubtedly more that I could have done with the women" (pp. 536–537). Civilising Subjects itself is unread. Distinct from the 1987 Family Fortunes contribution, which reaches gender history through edge_757's social-history claim and the existing roster row.

proposed_edges.relationship: The national “island story” rethought through empire: the history taught in schools and universities “needed to be rethought through the frame of empire” (2003)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read by the second research pass (JBS 42:4, 2003): race politics in postcolonial Britain "posed a challenge to the national story, the 'island story' of the homogeneity of the English-British nation" (p. 530); "One of my self-appointed tasks was to demonstrate the ways in which the well-established narrative of British history, the national history, the one taught in schools and universities, needed to be rethought through the frame of empire. Civilising Subjects is not only cultural and social history, it is also political history" (p. 537). Macaulay and Son (2012) extends the critique to Macaulay's History of England, as Tao Wei (Essays in History, 2014, read in full by the second pass) reads it: Hall calls him "one of the most influential proponents of liberal imperial discourse" (p. xiii); that book is unread and the edge rests on the 2003 statement.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Known only through Hall's reply; the commentators' texts are unread.
Her phrase “racial formation” does not cite Omi and Winant in the pages read (second pass).

Praise: "Hall’s excellent book"; a "dialectical" history; "empire is always on top of what it rules". Frames it with Culture and Imperialism's "overlapping territories" and "intertwined histories".
